bib.title: Pyserini: A Python Toolkit for Reproducible Information Retrieval Research with Sparse and Dense Representations

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Pyserini: A Python Toolkit for Reproducible Information Retrieval Research with Sparse and Dense Representations", Jimmy Lin, Xueguang Ma, Sheng-Chieh Lin, Jheng-Hong Yang, Ronak Pradeep, Rodrigo Nogueira (University of Waterloo). SIGIR '21 Resource Paper, 2021. PDF: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/lin-2021-pyserini.pdf

COVERAGE: The extraction is 48,644 chars. I read chars 0 to 40,000 in full, which covers the abstract, sections 1 to 5, Tables 1 and 2, the acknowledgements and references [1] to [8]. I skimmed chars 40,000 to 48,644 (the rest of the references) with a grep that printed entries [12], [13], [14], [15], [17], [18], [23], [26], [27], [28], [38] and [39], plus a few neighbouring lines. I did not read the other reference entries. The results sit entirely in the body.

CLAIMS
- claim: Pyserini is a pip-installable Python package. It ships queries, qrels, pre-built indexes and evaluation scripts for standard IR collections ("batteries are included").
  number: "approximately three dozen test collections"
  setup: v0.12.0
  quote: "Currently, Pyserini provides support for approximately three dozen test collections"
  where: p4, section 4
- claim: Sparse retrieval (BM25, bag of words) comes entirely from Lucene through Anserini. Dense and hybrid retrieval use Faiss, with HNSW for low-latency queries. Anserini itself has no dense or hybrid retrieval.
  number: none
  setup: toolkit architecture
  quote: "Sparse retrieval support in Pyserini comes entirely from Lucene (via Anserini). To support dense and hybrid retrieval, Pyserini integrates Facebook's Faiss library"
  where: p2
- claim: A single batch command reproduces the Anserini BM25 baseline from the MS MARCO leaderboard.
  number: MRR@10 0.1874 over 6,980 queries
  setup: MS MARCO passage dev subset, BM25 on the pre-built index
  quote: "The expected MRR@10 score is 0.1874 over 6980 queries."
  where: p4, section 3.3
- claim: On MS MARCO passage, BM25 is weakest, dense TCT-ColBERT is much stronger, and a weighted-interpolation hybrid beats both.
  number: dev MRR@10 / R@1k: BM25 default 0.184 / 0.853; dense HNSW 0.335 / 0.962; hybrid 0.353 / 0.970
  setup: MS MARCO passage (8.8M passages), dev set. BM25 default uses k1=0.9, b=0.4. Both hybrids used brute-force search.
  quote: "Original text 0.184 0.853 0.186 BM25, default (k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4)" / "(2b) TCT-ColBERT (HNSW) 0.335 0.962 -" / "(3a) TCT-ColBERT + original text 0.353 0.970 -"
  where: p5, Table 1
- claim: Tuning BM25 helps a little on the original text. Document expansion (doc2query-T5) gives a large gain while staying bag-of-words. Hybrid plus expansion is the best first-stage result.
  number: tuned BM25 0.187; doc2query-T5 default 0.272, tuned 0.282; hybrid + doc2query-T5 0.365 / R@1k 0.975
  setup: same dev set. Tuned values are k1=0.82, b=0.68 for the original text and k1=2.18, b=0.86 for doc2query-T5, found by grid search to maximise R@1k.
  quote: "(1b) Original text 0.187 0.857 0.190" / "(1d) doc2query–T5 0.282 0.951 -" / "TCT-ColBERT + doc2query–T5 0.365 0.975 -"
  where: p5, Table 1
- claim: Approximate HNSW search costs almost nothing in effectiveness compared with an exact brute-force scan.
  number: R@1k 0.964 brute-force vs 0.962 HNSW, with the same MRR@10
  setup: TCT-ColBERT, MS MARCO passage dev
  quote: "(2a) TCT-ColBERT (brute-force) 0.335 0.964 -"
  where: p5, Table 1
- claim: The dense index is about ten times the size of the sparse one, which the authors call a known weakness of dense retrieval.
  number: 2.6GB sparse vs 25GB dense
  setup: MS MARCO passage pre-built indexes
  quote: "the complete index, which includes a copy of all the texts, is a modest 2.6GB" / "the pre-built dense index is 25GB, which is substantially larger than the sparse index; this is a known weakness of dense retrieval techniques"
  where: p3
- claim: Pyserini's BM25 beats the BM25 baseline from the MS MARCO organisers.
  number: 0.167 dev / 0.165 test vs 0.184 / 0.186
  setup: MS MARCO passage
  quote: "(4a) BM25 (Microsoft Baseline) 0.167 - 0.165"
  where: p5, Table 1
- claim: The same ordering holds on MS MARCO document ranking: dense beats sparse, and the hybrid beats both, though the margins are smaller. Dense here is zero-shot, using the passage-trained encoder over a per-passage index with MaxP.
  number: dev MRR@100: tuned BM25 per-document 0.277; dense 0.332; hybrid 0.370; hybrid + doc2query 0.378
  setup: MS MARCO document dev set. Tuned BM25 uses k1=4.46, b=0.82.
  quote: "(1b) Original text (doc) 0.277 0.936 -" / "TCT-ColBERT 0.332 - -" / "(3a) TCT-ColBERT + original text 0.370 - -"
  where: p6, Table 2
- claim: With default BM25 parameters, per-document indexing looks much better than per-passage indexing. Once both are tuned, they are comparable.
  number: tuned 0.277 per-document vs 0.275 per-passage
  setup: MS MARCO document dev set
  quote: "(1d) Original text (passage) 0.275 0.931 0.246"
  where: p6, Table 2
- claim: Hybrid search is weighted interpolation of the sparse and dense scores, taken from the TCT-ColBERT implementation.
  number: none
  setup: HybridSearcher
  quote: "performs weighted interpolation on the individual results to arrive at a final ranking. This is a standard approach and Pyserini adopts the specific implementation in TCT-ColBERT [17]"
  where: p3, section 3.1
- claim: Reproducibility has a technical side (an internal end-to-end regression framework) and a social side (using their own tools and shared norms). Every Table 1 row from (1) to (3) is reproducible with the toolkit.
  number: none
  setup: none
  quote: "all results in rows (1) through (3) are reproducible with our toolkit"
  where: p4

LIMITS:
- The paper gives no latency or throughput numbers. HNSW is only described as "low latency".
- The interpolation weight for the hybrid is never stated, and reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is not tested.
- Training dense encoders is out of scope ("representational learning lies outside the scope of our toolkit").
- Support for dense retrieval over custom collections and access to dense internals are "less mature".
- Test-set numbers are missing for most dense and hybrid rows because the leaderboard limits submissions. Recall at 1k is reported on dev only.
- The authors concede the ANCE comparison on document ranking "isn't quite fair".
- Detailed treatment of reproducibility and future work is pushed to an arXiv extended version. The SIGIR paper gives only the short description in section 2, plus the conclusions.
- The pre-built MS MARCO indexes leave out positional data and document vectors.
- Dated: the paper uses v0.12.0. Its API names (SimpleSearcher, pyserini.dsearch, pyserini.hsearch) come from 2021, and later releases renamed them.
- Everything is evaluated on MS MARCO, with only the leaderboard models.

BUILDS ON: Anserini, Yang, Fang & Lin 2017 and 2018 [38, 39]; Lucene; Faiss, Johnson et al. 2017 [12]; HNSW, Malkov & Yashunin 2020 [23]; TCT-ColBERT, Lin et al. 2020 [17], distilled from ColBERT, Khattab & Zaharia 2020 [14]; DPR, Karpukhin et al. 2020 [13]; doc2query, Nogueira et al. 2019 [28]; docTTTTTquery, Nogueira & Lin 2019 [26]; the IR reproducibility challenge, Lin et al. 2016 [15]; MS MARCO, Bajaj et al. 2018 [6].

CODE (verbatim):
- p3, Figure 1:
  `searcher = SimpleSearcher.from_prebuilt_index('msmarco-passage')`
  `hits = searcher.search('what is a lobster roll?', 10)`
- p3, Figure 3: `hsearcher = HybridSearcher(dsearcher, ssearcher)`
- p4, section 3.3:
  `$ python -m pyserini.search --topics msmarco-passage-dev-subset --index msmarco-passage --output run.msmarco-passage.txt --bm25 --output-format msmarco`
  `$ python -m pyserini.eval.msmarco_passage_eval msmarco-passage-dev-subset run.msmarco-passage.txt`
- p4, Figure 4: `qrels = get_qrels('msmarco-passage-dev-subset')`

FIGURES:
- Figures 1 to 3 (p3) show sparse, dense and hybrid search, each in a few lines. Side by side, they show that hybrid is just two searchers composed.
- Figure 4 (p3) loads topics and qrels, which is useful for "Evaluating a retriever".
- Figure 5 (p4) gives IndexReader access to df/cf, postings and BM25 term weights, which suits the "library version" of BM25.
- Table 1 (p5) puts BM25, dense and hybrid side by side under one setup, which makes the comparison quickly.

PROBLEMS:
- Table 1's hybrid rows are both labelled "(3a)" in the extraction, while the prose calls the second one "(3b)".
- Table cell text is flattened in the extraction, but the values parse unambiguously.
- In the code listings, "␣" stands for a space. I rendered it as a plain space above.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
